title: What is time? (Confessions 11.14)
hook: if no one asks me, I know; if I try to explain, I don't
tomorrow: why would a strict monk's rulebook promise nothing harsh?

segments.voice: Late have I loved you: Augustine searching outside for a God who was within the whole time, calling through every sense. Now, a few pages on, he turns from his own story to a question that sounds easy.
screen: `LATE HAVE I LOVED THEE.` → `A QUESTION THAT SOUNDS EASY.`

segments.voice: A phone knows what time it is, to the second. Ask it what time is, and it hands back a definition that explains nothing. Augustine is at that exact spot, pen in hand, deep in the Confessions. He has just been talking to God about the first line of Genesis, a beginning before any clock. Then he stops and asks it plainly: what, then, is time? Nothing, he says, do we talk about more easily. Late, soon, yesterday, someday, a long while, a moment ago. So he tries to answer, and what comes out is a confession of a different kind.
screen: `A PHONE KNOWS THE TIME.` → `WHAT, THEN, IS TIME?` → `LATE, SOON, SOMEDAY.`

segments.voice: If no one asks me, I know. If I try to explain it to someone who asks, I don't. Then he works the puzzle out loud. The past isn't anymore. The future isn't yet. So only the present is. But if the present stayed present and never slid into the past, it wouldn't be time at all. It would be eternity. So the present only is, he says, because it's on its way to not being. He isn't playing with words, and he isn't showing off. Book Eleven is reading Genesis, "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth," and the God he's praying to doesn't live in passing time. A little further on, Augustine finds where past and future actually live: in the mind, now. A present of things past, which is memory. A present of things present, which is attention. A present of things future, which is expectation. Here's the one to tell a friend tonight: in Augustine's picture, nobody ever visits yesterday or tomorrow. We only remember and hope, and both happen right now. The carry gives that a short shape, though the text never turns it into a slogan. It leaves Augustine still asking God to help him understand, standing in the one moment that is.
screen: `IF NO ONE ASKS ME, I KNOW.` · `THE PAST IS GONE; THE FUTURE ISN'T YET.` · `A PRESENT THAT STAYED WOULD BE ETERNITY.` · `MEMORY, ATTENTION, EXPECTATION.` · then, large: `NOW IS ALL WE HAVE.`

segments.voice: Listen for one sound in the room: a fan, traffic, your own breathing. Each time you catch it, it's already passing and already new. When your mind runs off to yesterday or later, call it memory or hope, and come back to the sound.
What is time? Augustine's question in Book Eleven: easy until someone asks, and only the passing present truly here.
Keep this: now is all we have, with the past held as memory and the future as hope. See you tomorrow.

match.prompt: what is time? — tap the pairs.

myth: Augustine says time is just an illusion
the popular version. he says he knows it until asked, and finds past and future present in the mind.
Augustine says a present that never passed would be eternity
if the present stayed present, it wouldn't be time at all.
Augustine can explain time easily to anyone who asks
if no one asks, he knows; when he tries to explain, he doesn't.

fork.setup: at dinner, your grandpa keeps saying 'back in my day' and your sister keeps saying 'when i move out.' by Augustine, where are they both?
options: one is stuck in the past, one in the future; neither is here.
both are here: one remembering, one hoping, right now.
nowhere; only clocks really hold time.
fork.reveal: for Augustine, the past lives now as memory and the future now as expectation. both of them are at the table.

original.note: Latin: time. Augustine's question in Confessions 11.14 is quid est ergo tempus? what then is time?

trapdoor: what you thought: everyone knows what time is.
what it means: Augustine knows until he's asked: the past is gone, the future not yet, and the present keeps passing.
what a scholar hears: Book Eleven reads Genesis, in the beginning, and Augustine goes on to name three presents in the mind: memory, attention, expectation.
guess: Augustine's question about what passing time really is
a question about managing a crowded schedule
a riddle about the clocks monks kept for prayer
recall: God was within; he searched outside
the whole life given, set alight

chat.says: testimony's DONE. now every adult asks 'so what's next?' and i'm mentally already in august
options: August is a hope, and you're hoping it right now. Augustine would say: be here for it.
Plan harder. For Augustine the future is the only time that really counts.
Look back instead. For Augustine the past is the only time that lasts.
chat.meaning: For Augustine, the future lives in the mind now, as expectation. The only place to hope, remember or notice is the present.

Augustine.meaning: a bishop whose Confessions is a long prayer to God

Confessions.meaning: Augustine's book: his life story told to God

Genesis.meaning: the Bible's first book, which opens with creation

eternity.meaning: God's life outside passing time, in Augustine's picture

sources.quoted: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.

notes: All Confessions lines are paraphrased (quoted: null); the Pusey (1838) wording was not checked word for word.

Beats from 11.14: 'What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not'; nothing mentioned more familiarly; past no longer is, future not yet; a present always present would be eternity; time is only because it tends not to be. From 11.20: a present of things past (memory), present of things present (sight/attention), present of things future (expectation). Confirm each.
'Book Eleven is reading Genesis': Book 11 begins Augustine's reading of Genesis 1:1 (continued in Books 12–13); confirm the phrasing.

The carry 'now is all we have' is the index line, not Augustine's words; the teach says plainly that the text doesn't turn it into a slogan. A Keeper may want to check the carry doesn't overstate Augustine.
Myth item 'time is just an illusion' is marked false as the popular misreading; Augustine says past and future are not, yet are present in the mind. Confirm the reveal is fair.
Hook added in v3: the phone image is the lesson's own; 'a long while, a moment ago' loosely echoes 11.14's everyday time words (a long time, a short time); confirm.
